The Keeper's Log

For most of the nineteenth century, a lighthouse keeper's day was measured in wicks, oil and weather. The log they kept was part diary, part ledger and part warning to whoever came next.

A day on the rock

The lamp was lit at sunset and trimmed every four hours until dawn. Between watches the keeper polished the lens, wound the clockwork that turned it, and wrote down the wind, the sea state and every ship that passed. A well-kept log in 1848 might note a café owner's rowing boat bringing bread, or a storm that kept the relief crew away for nine days.

Keepers didn't write for pleasure. The entries were short and plain, because the next keeper had to read them quickly by lamplight and act on them.

What the log recorded

  • The time the lamp was lit and put out
  • Oil used, wicks replaced and panes cleaned
  • Wind direction, visibility and the state of the sea
  • Ships sighted, signals exchanged and wrecks reported

Fog from the north-east at four. Horn sounded until nine. Nothing passed.

Reading an old log today

Historians now use these books to rebuild old weather records. The Greek word φάρος and the Japanese 灯台 both mean lighthouse, and archives around the world hold logs written in dozens of languages.

A typical entry in a transcription tool looks like this:

1848-11-02  sunset 16:41  wind NE 5  vis. poor  lamp lit 16:30
